Bloomberg September 02, 2026 / 15:47 IST Viktor Orban Hungary plans a wealth tax on assets over 1 billion forint. New government aims to raise revenue and reduce inequality. Tax could generate 300-600 billion forint annually. Did our AI summary help? Market Mastery Webinar by Vishal Malkan Find the weak links in your portfolio by Vishal Malkan Register for FREE Webinar Register for FREE Hungary’s government plans to introduce a wealth tax on assets exceeding 1 billion forint ($3.1 million), according to a senior official, reaffirming Prime Minister Peter Magyar’s bid to raise levies on the country’s richest. “The wealth tax will be a milestone,” Cabinet Minister Balint Ruff told the Telex news website in an interview published on Wednesday. “The regulation has been ready for a long time and it will impose a wealth tax on income and assets exceeding 1 billion forint.” Magyar’s Tisza party won a landslide election in April, ending 16 years of Viktor Orban’s rule that saw inequality rise and widespread corruption enrich a new politically-connected class. The premier said in June that the wealth tax may bring in annual revenue of 300 billion to 600 billion forint and would be introduced from next year. Wealth levy proposals are gaining ground on both sides of the Atlantic as politicians seek to boost funding and reduce inequality. California is weighing a billionaires tax, New York has floated several new levies on the wealthy and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also added to speculation that taxes may need to rise. Read More: Sweden’s Rich Weigh Exit as Wealth Tax Proposals Gain Momentum The experience with wealth taxes is mixed. Sweden’s rich are weighing options to protect their assets and even to leave the country as political parties push for such a levy. Neighboring Norway raised taxes on the wealthy after a left-leaning government took power in 2021, prompting some of its wealthiest residents to move abroad. A government-mandated commission there has recommended steep cuts in the wealth tax to mend the business climate. Ruff didn’t give details about the Hungarian wealth levy, such as the tax rate or what sort of assets would be subject to it. The government in Budapest needs additional revenue as it faces one of widest budget shortfalls in the European Union, estimated at 7.5% of economic output in this year’s amended fiscal plan. But Magyar said in June that the aim of the tax wasn’t “punitive” but to broaden social responsibility in a country where a flat personal income tax has been criticized for being burdensome on the poor and lenient on the wealthiest. https://www.politico.eu/article/romania-.text: Romania ended five months of political paralysis Tuesday with its parliament voting in Luca Niculescu as prime minister after three failed attempts to form a government — but the deal comes with a six-month deadline for the parties to strike a more lasting agreement. The threat of snap elections, which would likely see the populist right-wing Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) party surge, helped push the center-right National Liberal Party (PNL) and the center-left Social Democrats (PSD) to agree on a government led by independent Niculescu, a former journalist and diplomat who was nominated as prime minister by moderate President Nicușor Dan earlier this month. The socialists will join the cabinet, but the liberals will stay out. Romania has the sixth-largest population in the EU and plays a critical role in NATO’s defense of southeastern Europe as home to a major military base and a U.S. missile shield site. The country has been plagued by political instability and a mushrooming budget deficit in recent years, fueling a surge in support for hard-right nationalist politics. Advertisement Advertisement The new deal keeping the government afloat expires in six months, and parties will need to renegotiate the pact with no agreement yet on what comes next. During this period, the Social Democrats will try to pass an investment-focused 2027 budget by the end of November, steering Bucharest away from austerity, party leader Sorin Grindeanu told POLITICO Playbook Capitals in an interview . “Romania needs an economic recovery plan, not austerity,” he said. “Our priorities are protecting purchasing power and supporting business, restarting public investment, and improving essential public services.” Grindeanu added that he aims to revise the 2026 budget by the end of October and to fast-track implementation of EU projects to unblock funds. The Social Democrats in May teamed up with AUR to topple the coalition government led by centrists and centre-right liberals, as unpopular debt-cutting reforms drove Social Democrat voters toward the populist right. PNL and USR have refused to govern with the Social Democrats again. The formation of the new government makes snap elections harder to trigger once the six-month deal expires, as Romania’s constitution requires two failed attempts to install a government before Parliament can be dissolved. Grindeanu hopes to persuade his former coalition partners to reunite in six months, but with a different economic program. Fearing an uptick in support for the far right, he wants to avoid further cuts. Advertisement Advertisement But the pivot away from austerity puts him at odds with the PNL, which has defended fiscal restraint. The PNL refused to sign a detailed coalition program, Grindeanu said, forcing the administration to cobble together support vote by vote over the next six months. Grindeanu distinguished between parliamentary votes and lasting alliances, and said he won’t seek a pact with AUR, citing deep disagreements over Europe and national security. He said he rejected an offer from AUR to back a €300 million social spending package during negotiations over the 2026 budget, after the far-right party demanded PSD’s support on another, unspecified issue in return. Instead, he waited to find a compromise with PNL. “Until I will stay in this position, PSD will not have any agreement with AUR,” he vowed.
